name: Aaron Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes out with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I finish about 200 beef cattle a year and grow wheat, barley and oilseed on our own 90 hectares. On top of that I farm another 150 hectares on contract for two retired neighbours, Mr Doyle and Mrs Fenn, who pay me to do all their field work. A normal day is the cattle at half six, then out on the tractor, which steers itself by GPS now, so I can check grain prices on my phone while it drives. My wife Grace teaches at the primary school, and our two, Daniel and Esther, are at the secondary and the primary.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does AI fit into your work today?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use it every day. It tracks the cattle weights from the scales, tells me when to sell grain, writes the invoices for the contract work and checks the weather against my spraying plans. I'm on the church council, and the older men tease me about my phone. I trust my phone more than the grain merchant, though not more than the Lord. I'd say it saves me ten hours a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a pity, because I was hoping for more. What we've got already earns its keep, so I'd keep using it. I'd tell the men at church they can stop worrying about robots and start worrying about the weather again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. The contract work for Mr Doyle and Mrs Fenn brings in steady money, Grace's teaching salary is secure, and the cattle are paying this year. I've a mortgage and only a few months saved, but the business is ticking along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, with the tools I already use. I'd buy the second-hand GPS drill I've had my eye on, about 18,000, because it'd save diesel and seed on the contract ground. And I'd ask Mr Doyle for a five-year contract instead of a year at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit disappointed. Like a good harvest that could have been a great one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said only a few months saved. Doesn't that worry you with a mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would if Grace's job wasn't there. Her salary covers the mortgage, and the farm covers the rest. The money that worries me is borrowing for the drill, so I'd only do it once Mr Doyle signs the longer contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a longer contract with Mr Doyle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Mr Doyle is 79, and if he passes on, his nephew might sell the land. A five-year deal means I'm still farming Mr Doyle's fields whoever owns them. It's good business and it's fair to both of us.

say: I was hoping for more, but what we have **earns its keep**.
The men at church can stop worrying about robots and **worry about weather**.
think: I'd be **fine**: contract work, Grace's salary and the cattle all pay.
A **mortgage** and a few months saved are covered by the business ticking along.
do: Buy a **second-hand GPS drill** for about 18,000 once the contract is signed.
Ask Mr Doyle for a **five-year contract** instead of yearly.
Carry on with the **AI tools** I already use daily.
feel: **Calm**, a bit disappointed, like a good harvest that could have been great.
S0.quote: A five-year deal means I'm still farming Mr Doyle's fields whoever owns them.
fieldNote: Aaron sounds **secure**, with contract income and his wife's steady salary.
He's **disappointed** that AI stalls, which reflects his appetite for it.
He weighs **borrowing** carefully against a longer contract.
His faith and his **business sense** sit side by side comfortably.

steps.text: Buy a second-hand GPS drill for about 18,000
Get Mr Doyle to sign a five-year contract for his fields

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the good kind of change, and I'd say it to anyone. Farmers who use it will do better, and that's how a market should work. I'd also say young people need apprenticeships in this, not just university courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. The thinking side of my business, selling grain, buying inputs, invoicing, planning the contract work, is maybe a quarter of my week. AI already does some of it, and in this picture it does nearly all of it, which frees me to take on more land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand the grain selling, the input buying and the invoicing to AI completely this winter. I'd use the time saved to offer contract farming to two more retired neighbours, which could add 100 hectares. And I'd look at a used robot weeder for the oilseed once a couple of local farms have tried them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Busy, a bit restless, ready to get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who loses out in this picture, from where you stand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The grain merchant's office staff, for a start, and the young woman at the feed company who takes my orders. I feel for them, I do. My father told me to learn a trade that needs your hands and your head together, and I'd say the same to the young woman at the feed company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd take on more land. Can you do that with a few months of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Contract farming doesn't need much money up front, which is why I like it. The neighbours own the land and I bring the machines and the know-how. The risk is breakdowns, so I'd put 2,000 aside as a repair fund before I sign anyone new.

say: This is **the good kind** of change, and farmers who use it will do better.
Young people need **apprenticeships** in this, not just university courses.
think: The **thinking side** of my business is about a quarter of my week.
AI doing nearly all of it frees me to **take on more land**.
do: Hand **grain selling**, buying and invoicing fully to AI this winter.
Offer **contract farming** to two more neighbours, adding about 100 hectares.
Put **2,000** aside as a repair fund before signing anyone new.
feel: **Good**: busy, a bit restless and ready to get on with it.
S1.quote: My father told me to learn a trade that needs your hands and your head together, and I'd say the same to the young woman at the feed company.
fieldNote: Aaron sees Steady Disruption as **good business** and plans to grow.
He shows **sympathy** for office workers but frames it as self-reliance.
His growth plan is **low-cost** contract farming, backed by a repair fund.
His free-market view is clear: **those who adapt** do better.

steps.text: Hand grain selling, input buying and invoicing to AI
Offer contract farming to two more retired neighbours
Put 2,000 aside as a repair fund before new contracts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, so let's not waste time complaining. I'd tell farmers at church and the mart to get ready for robots, because 2031 will come round fast. I'd also say the government should keep out of the way and let farmers buy what they need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one worries me more than I'd let on. My contract work depends on retired neighbours needing someone with machines, and by 2031 a big contractor with a robot fleet could do their fields cheaper than me. I'd have to get robots myself first, which means borrowing with only a few months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2028 I'd let AI run every bit of the paperwork and selling, and spend the time learning everything I can about field robots. I'd save hard, maybe 400 a month, so I have a deposit ready by 2030. And the moment decent robots exist, I'd lease two and offer robot contracting to every farm within twenty kilometres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more excited than scared. Like the night before harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is mostly hands-on, and robots arrive about three years after AGI. What do you do with those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those three years are the whole game for me. Thinking AI makes my office work free in 2028, but nobody has robots in the field yet, so the contracting is still mine. If I've got the money and the know-how ready by 2031, I'm the robot contractor, not the farmer who loses out to one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Grace think about leasing robots with a thin cushion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace would say pray about it and do the sums twice, and she'd be right on both. Her salary is our safety net, so we'd agree never to borrow more than the farm can repay on its own. If the robots don't pay, I hand them back after a year.

say: The change is here, so **don't waste time** complaining.
Government should keep **out of the way** and let farmers buy what they need.
think: A **robot contractor** could take my neighbours' work cheaper by 2031.
Getting robots first means **borrowing** with only a few months saved.
do: Save **400 a month** for a robot deposit by 2030.
Lease **two field robots** as soon as decent ones exist.
Offer **robot contracting** to every farm within twenty kilometres.
feel: **Anxious** but more excited than scared, like the night before harvest.
S2.quote: If I've got the money and the know-how ready by 2031, I'm the robot contractor, not the farmer who loses out to one.
fieldNote: Aaron is privately **more worried** than he'd say in public.
He reads the three-year gap as **the whole game** for his contracting.
His **wife Grace** sets the borrowing limit, which he accepts.
He'd rather **be the disruptor** than lose to one.

steps.text: Save 400 a month toward a robot deposit by 2030
Lease two field robots as soon as decent ones exist
Offer robot contracting to farms within twenty kilometres
Let AI run all paperwork and grain selling from 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people stop dithering. I'd tell young farmers to get into robot apprenticeships now. And I'd say it's families and businesses that will sort this, not government schemes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. AI in 2031 takes my paperwork, and robots in 2034 give me time to save rather than borrow, and to test machines properly. The danger is still a big contractor, but I'd have years to tie my neighbours into longer contracts first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get every contract customer onto a five-year agreement by 2029. I'd save for robots instead of borrowing, about 300 a month, and buy the first one outright around 2033. And I'd sit down with Daniel about an apprenticeship in agricultural engineering, because robots will need people who understand both farms and machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. A steady sort of excitement, with a little caution in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Daniel want that apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel loves taking things apart, so I think yes, but I'd let him choose. Esther wants to be a teacher like Grace, and I'd say good, children will still need teachers. I'd never force either of them onto the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been calm in most pictures. Is there anything you're not saying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that I'm 43 and I've never failed at anything big, so maybe I'm too confident. Grace says pride comes before a fall, and she quotes the Bible at me when she says it. I'd take that seriously.

say: Five years is enough to get ready if people **stop dithering**.
**Families and businesses** will sort this out, not government schemes, and young farmers need robot apprenticeships.
think: I think **I'd do well**, saving rather than borrowing for robots.
I'd have years to tie neighbours into **longer contracts** first.
do: Get every contract customer onto a **five-year agreement** by 2029.
Save **300 a month** and buy the first robot outright around 2033.
Talk to Daniel about an **agricultural engineering** apprenticeship.
feel: **Good**, with steady excitement and a little caution.
S3.quote: I'm 43 and I've never failed at anything big, so maybe I'm too confident.
fieldNote: Aaron is **upbeat**, but admits he may be too confident.
He'd **lock in contracts** and save rather than borrow.
He'd encourage but **not force** his children's choices.
The **big contractor** threat keeps him from full calm.

steps.text: Put every contract customer on a five-year agreement by 2029
Save 300 a month and buy a first robot outright
Talk to Daniel about an agricultural engineering apprenticeship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who's caught out had fair warning. I'd tell farmers to make one good decision a year rather than panic in year nine. And I'd say the land will still need people who care about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be calm in this one. AI in 2036 and robots in 2039, when I'm 56 with the mortgage nearly paid and the kids grown. I'd have twelve years of using AI every day behind me, so I'd be ahead of nearly everyone round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd keep doing what I'm doing, using AI daily and running the cattle and contract work. I'd add one new bit of automation each year, starting with automatic weighing and feeding in the cattle shed. And I'd make sure Daniel and Esther are both on a path that suits a world with robots in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really, with a bit of impatience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep mentioning patience and impatience. Which wins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Impatience, most days, which is why I'm glad Grace is there. Ten years means I can do things in the right order, and the right order matters more than speed. I'd rather build the farm well than build it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Doyle and Mrs Fenn, if they're still alive, and the older farmers at church who won't touch a phone. I'd want to make sure they're not left behind. Maybe I'd run their fields with my robots and charge them fairly, like a good neighbour should.

say: Ten years is **plenty**, and anyone caught out had fair warning.
Make **one good decision** a year rather than panic in year nine.
think: I'd be **calm**, at 56 with the mortgage nearly paid.
Twelve years of **daily AI use** puts me ahead of nearly everyone.
do: Keep running the cattle and **contract work** as now.
Add one automation a year, starting with **automatic weighing and feeding**.
Help Daniel and Esther onto paths that suit **a world with robots**.
feel: **Calm and content**, with a bit of impatience.
S4.quote: I'd rather build the farm well than build it first.
fieldNote: Aaron is **calm** here, with time, experience and a paid-down mortgage.
He values **doing things in order**, a lesson he credits to Grace.
He feels a **neighbourly duty** to older farmers who won't use technology.
His children's **futures** are part of his planning.

steps.text: Keep running 200 cattle and the contract work as now
Fit automatic weighing and feeding in the cattle shed
Steer Daniel and Esther toward careers that suit robots

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to borrow before I'm ready and race the big contractors with a few months of savings. What would help is fair access to leasing for small operators, not grants, just leases on the same terms the big firms get. And plain information about which robots actually work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the neighbours. Farming here works because people help each other at harvest and in bad winters. If robots mean nobody needs a neighbour any more, we lose something no machine gives back.

headlineQuote: If robots mean nobody needs a neighbour any more, we lose something no machine gives back.
portrait: Aaron Okafor is a 43-year-old **beef and arable farmer** who also contract-farms for retired neighbours.
He uses **AI every day** and wants more of it, trusting markets over government.
He's calm in the mild pictures, but **fast AGI** forces him to borrow before he's ready.
With more time he'd **save, not borrow**, and lock neighbours into longer contracts.
His wife Grace and his faith **keep his confidence** in check.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, borrowing too early to race big contractors.
whatWouldHelp: Fair **leasing terms** for small operators, not grants.
